title: Rep. Dontavius L. Jarrells voted Yea on HB433, a bill revising Ohio amusement ride laws
text:
Rep. Dontavius L. Jarrells voted Yea on HB433, a bill revising Ohio amusement ride laws
Rep. Dontavius L. Jarrells (D-1st) voted Yea on HB433, a bill revising Ohio’s amusement ride laws, which passed the Ohio House 87-6 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill revises Ohio’s amusement ride laws by updating the definition of amusement rides to exclude manufactured rock climbing walls in regulated climbing facilities and rides operated only at trade shows, and by refining ride classifications used to set annual inspection and reinspection fees. The bill restructures the fee schedule to distinguish kiddie, family, major, spectacular, family or portable roller coasters, tower rides and large roller coasters, and directs the agriculture director to define these categories by rule. It maintains permit, inspection and insurance requirements and keeps all collected fees in the amusement ride inspection fund.
HB433 was introduced by Rep. Roy Klopfenstein and Rep. Sarah Fowler Arthur.
Jarrells, born and raised in Cleveland, Ohio, earned his Bachelor of Arts in Political Science with a minor in Economics from Hiram College in 2010. He was elected as State Representative for House District 25 in 2020 and is currently serving his second term as Representative for House District 1, where he advocates for policies such as the Paystub Protection Act and the Foster-to-College Scholarship Act.
Jarrells has held various roles in public service, including an Ohio Legislative Service Commission Fellow during the 129th General Assembly and positions with the Ohio Association of County Behavioral Health Authorities and Ohio Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services. He serves as the Assistant Minority Leader for the Ohio House Democratic Caucus and is involved in several state and national organizations, including the Ohio Commission on Minority Health.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
